title: Definite and indefinite articles
goal: By the end of this lesson you can choose between le, la, l', les and un, une, des, use the article to show a noun's gender and number, and recognise the gender Quebecers give to common English borrowings like une job.

learn.h: Every French noun has a gender
body: In French, every noun is either masculine or feminine, even objects: *le livre* (the book) is masculine, *la table* (the table) is feminine. The gender is not logical, so learn every noun together with its article.

The article is usually the only thing that tells you the gender and number of a noun when you hear it, because the plural *-s* is silent: *le livre* and *les livres* sound different only in the article.
learn.tip: Never learn 'livre = book'. Learn 'un livre = a book'.

body: *le* goes before a masculine noun, *la* before a feminine noun, and *les* before any plural noun.
Before a vowel or a silent h, *le* and *la* both become *l'*: *l'ami*, *l'école*, *l'hôtel*. In *les*, the s links to a vowel with a [z] sound: *les‿amis*.

learn.h: The indefinite article: a, an, some
body: *un* goes before a masculine noun, *une* before a feminine noun, and *des* before any plural noun. *Des* means 'some', but English often leaves it out: *J'ai des amis* = I have (some) friends.
*un* and *des* make a liaison before a vowel: *un‿ami* [n], *des‿amis* [z]. *Une* never changes.
learn.tip: French almost never drops the article. 'I have friends' must be 'J'ai des amis'.

body: Use *un / une / des* for something new or not specific: *Il y a un chat* (there's a cat). Use *le / la / les* for something specific or already mentioned: *Le chat est noir* (the cat is black).
French also uses *le / la / les* for things in general, where English uses no article: *J'aime le café* (I like coffee), *Les chats sont gentils* (cats are nice).

learn.h: Quebec: English words get a gender too
body: Quebec French borrows English words in casual speech, and each one gets a gender. Some differ from France: Quebecers say *une job* (feminine), while France says *un job*. You will also hear *une game* (a game, a match), *un party* and *une toune* (a song, from 'tune').

Note: *un char* (a car) is often called an anglicism, but it isn't. *Char* is an old French word for a cart or carriage, kept in Quebec for 'car'. It is informal; the standard word is *une voiture* (also *une auto*, very common in Quebec).

quebec.intro: Casual Quebec French uses many English loanwords, and each gets a gender, sometimes different from France: une job. Un char (car) looks like one but is actually an old French word.

informal; char is old French, not English

French needs an article; des = some.

speak.prompt: Name five objects around you with un or une.
speak.model: Un livre, une table, une chaise, un téléphone, une lampe.

speak.prompt: Now say something about each one with le or la.
speak.model: Le livre est petit. La table est grande. La lampe est blanche.

speak.prompt: Say three things you like, using le, la or les.
speak.model: J'aime le café, la neige et les chats.

write.prompt: Write 4–6 sentences about your street or your home: what there is (un, une, des) and what it is like (le, la, les).
write.model: J'habite dans une petite rue. Il y a une école et un café. L'école est grande. Le café est très bon. Il y a des enfants dans la rue. J'aime la rue.
